title: Adab of knowledge
hook: a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet and teaches by asking

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of sleep, and your line: sleep with remembrance. What was your last word last night? Today, the manners of learning, which is what this whole path has been doing. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab tells it, in Sahih Muslim. They were sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a man walked in. Very white clothes. Very black hair. No dust of travel on him, and nobody there knew who he was. He sat down right in front of the Prophet, rested his knees against the Prophet's knees, laid his palms on his thighs, and began to ask questions. Only later did the Prophet tell them who it was. Jibril, the angel, who had come to teach them their religion. He taught by asking.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `HE TAUGHT BY ASKING.`

segments.voice: That scene holds the adab of knowledge in its posture. Jibril came to teach, and he came looking like a student. He sat close. He was still. He asked, and listened to the answers. Respect for the one you learn from isn't flattery. It's how you sit. The Qur'an shows the same thing with a prophet. In surah al-Kahf, Moses meets a servant of Allah who has knowledge he doesn't, a man tradition calls al-Khidr. And Moses, himself a prophet, asks, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you can teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? He's told he'll need patience. He agrees, and then struggles to keep quiet. The humility goes all the way up. In surah Ta Ha, the Prophet himself is told to ask for more, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Nobody in these passages has finished learning. Then the last piece, and it's the sharp one. Surah al-Saff, Pickthall again: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?" And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says, in paraphrase, that on the Day of Rising a person's feet won't move until they're asked about their life, their wealth, their body, and their knowledge: what did you do with it? Not how much did you know. What did you do with it. Knowledge, in this adab, isn't a collection. It's a debt that gets paid in action. Sit close. Ask for more. Then go and do the thing.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CAME AS A STUDENT.` · `A PROPHET ASKS TO FOLLOW.` · `MY LORD, INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `WHAT DID YOU DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: The practice: act on something you learned. Settle, and breathe. Look back over these last days: the kindlier word, the near side of the dish, leaving room, honoring the guest, the line before a trip, the last word before sleep. Or anything else you've learned lately. Pick one you've heard and haven't yet done. Just one. Now decide exactly when today it will happen, and see yourself doing it. If you pray, you can say the line from Ta Ha: my Lord, increase me in knowledge. The bell holds the time.
Adab of knowledge. The manners of learning: honor the one who teaches, stay humble enough to ask for more, and act on what you know. Today's word.
Your line: learn, then do. Before today ends, take the one thing you chose and do it, even in a small way. Tomorrow, the adab of the road. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Muslim students are taught to honor their teachers, to recite "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge," and to treat knowledge as something to act on, citing the hadith of Jibril and the hadith of what a person did with what they knew.

fork.setup: you're Moses, a prophet, and you meet a man with knowledge you don't have. what do you do?
options: teach him what you know first.
ask if you may follow him and learn.
walk on; you're already a prophet.
fork.reveal: in al-Kahf, Moses asks to follow and be taught, and is told he'll need patience.

original.note: Arabic: knowledge; it begins with the throat letter 'ayn.

trapdoor: what you thought: the adab of knowledge means being polite in class.
what it means: honoring the one who teaches, staying humble enough to ask for more, and turning what you learn into what you do.
what a scholar hears: Jibril's knees against the Prophet's knees in Sahih Muslim, and al-Tirmidhi's question about knowledge: what did you do with it?

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril, told by 'Umar)
Qur'an 18:65–70 (Moses asks to follow and be taught; patience)

sources.quoted: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge.
O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2417 (the feet won't move until asked: life, knowledge, wealth, body)

notes: Sahih Muslim 8 and Tirmidhi 2417 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details (white clothes, black hair, no sign of travel, knees and palms).
Al-Khidr is not named in the Qur'an; the teach says 'a man tradition calls al-Khidr'. Confirm phrasing.
Editor: 'nobody in the scene' changed to 'nobody in these passages', since Moses, Ta Ha and the Jibril hadith are separate texts, not one scene.
